title: TikTok pack 2 (11 originals, Shorts v4, Andrew)
_note: TikTok pack 2, Shorts v4 (research/45; Studio, 2026-10-25). 11 TikTok-only originals: 6 single-animal deep dives at 61-75 s (one per posting day) and 5 Shorts at 20-25 s. Deep dives except the secretarybird (rendered first) use the open-loop structure (research/40, Mayor 10/25): a withheld answer promised in lines 1-3, two wrong guesses ("decoy"), the "payoff" at 50-80% of the words; all pass tools/openloop.py. None of the animals appear in pack 1 or any earlier script. Meatball tries something, it goes wrong, the true fact is the punchline; the animal is a whole-animal cut-out that acts on the word (beat "animal"). Lines are 8 words or fewer. Asks (like, follow, comment) are in Meatball's voice and never in the first 3 s. No quiz cards, no read-outs. Every "at" anchor is a word, never a bare number (tools/v3.py reads numbers as seconds). Voice: en-US-AndrewMultilingualNeural at +0% then atempo 1.10 (= +10%), the free v3/v4 voice. Photos: iNaturalist research-grade, wild (captive=false), CC0/CC BY only, first photo of the pinned observation, scanned with animal.subject() and then checked by eye one by one (whole animal, alive, right species, no halo, nothing missing). Facts web-checked 10/25 with sources on each hook beat; '_len' marks short/deep.

beats.say: This bird kicks snakes to death.
beats.loop_say: So never ask it for a lesson. Because
beats.short_title: Secretary Birds Kick Snakes to Death 🦵
beats.comment: Would you take a kick lesson from this bird? 👇
beats.bonus: A 2016 force-plate study clocked the kick at about 195 newtons with just 15 ms of contact.
sources: Portugal, Murn, Sparkes & Daley 2016, Current Biology 26: R58-R59, 'The fast and forceful kicking strike of the secretary bird' (captive male named Madeleine, Hawk Conservancy Trust; rubber snake over a force plate; ~195 N = ~5x body weight; mean contact 15 ms; strikes rely on pre-planned aim, too fast to correct mid-kick) — https://pure.royalholloway.ac.uk/en/publications/the-fast-and-forceful-kicking-strike-of-the-secretary-bird/ ; summary https://phys.org/news/2016-01-snake-hunting-secretary-birds-body-weight.html

Wikipedia, Secretarybird (about 1.3 m / 4 ft 3 in tall; hunts on foot, walking at about 120 steps a minute; small vertebrates and insects, venomous snakes such as adders and cobras regularly eaten; on the coats of arms of South Africa and Sudan; IUCN Endangered since 2020) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretarybird (checked 2026-10-25)
A human blink lasts about 100-150 ms (Harvard Database of Useful Biological Numbers, BNID 100706) — https://bionumbers.hms.harvard.edu/bionumber.aspx?id=100706
beats.caption: Secretary birds hunt on foot and stomp their prey. Scientists measured one kick at about five times the bird's body weight, landing in 15 milliseconds. #secretarybird #birds #animalfacts #wildlife

beats.say: So naturally, I asked for a lesson.
It's about four feet tall.
Mostly legs.
Scientists measured its kick.
They used a rubber snake.
And a bird named Madeleine.
Madeleine is a boy.
Nobody tell Madeleine.
Then Madeleine kicked me.
Five times its own body weight.
The kick lasted fifteen milliseconds.
That's faster than a blink.
I never saw it coming.
Neither did the rubber snake.
Tap like. It's for my bruises.
It hunts on foot, all day.
About 120 steps a minute.
My legs are literally sticks.
Lizards. Rodents. Insects. Snakes.
Even cobras and adders.
It aims first. Then it stomps.
Too fast to correct mid-kick.
If it misses, it kicks again.
I am rolling away now.
Now the weird part.
It's on South Africa's coat of arms.
And Sudan's.
A national symbol. For kicking.
I'm only on menus.
Sadly, it's now endangered.
So I'm rooting for it.
From very far away.
Follow me. I'll be in these bushes.
Threat to meatballs: extreme.
Would you take a kick lesson? Comment.
Archerfish shoot bugs down with water.
beats.loop_say: So never stand on a leaf. Because
beats.short_title: Archerfish Shoot Bugs Down With Water 💦
beats.comment: Would you trust a fish that remembers your face? 👇
beats.bonus: In a 2016 Scientific Reports study, trained archerfish picked a learned human face out of 44 new ones.
sources: Australian Geographic, 'Smart fish that spit' (archerfish knock ants and other insects off overhanging foliage with water jets, from up to two metres away) — https://www.australiangeographic.com.au/topics/wildlife/2017/08/smart-fish-that-spit

Newport et al. 2016, Scientific Reports (archerfish trained to spit at one face picked it out of 44 new faces, ~81-86% accuracy, greyscale oval-cropped images) — https://www.cbc.ca/news/science/fish-can-recognize-faces-1.3629421 ; https://e360.yale.edu/digest/fish_can_recognize_human_faces
beats.caption: Archerfish spit jets of water to knock insects off leaves, up to about two meters away. They can even learn to tell human faces apart. #archerfish #fish #animalfacts #science

beats.say: So I stood on a leaf above one.
It spat.
From up to two meters away.
Bugs fall. Meatballs too.
It can even learn human faces.
It found one face among forty-four strangers.
So it knows my face now.
I don't even have a good side.
Like and follow. I'm drying off.
Would you dodge it? Comment.
Tokay geckos can climb almost anything.
beats.loop_say: So now I live in a frying pan. Because
beats.short_title: The One Thing a Gecko Can't Stick To 🦎
beats.comment: What did you guess the surface was? 👇
beats.bonus: Gecko toes stick with van der Waals forces from millions of tiny spatulae; nonstick coatings and wet surfaces undermine the grip.
sources: Wikipedia, Tokay gecko (25-30 cm total length on average, some about 40 cm; the name imitates the male's call; aggressive and territorial, can inflict a strong bite, larger ones can pierce skin; foot pads support the whole body on a vertical surface; nocturnal; established outside its range in Florida; eats insects and small vertebrates) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokay_gecko (checked 2026-10-25)

National Geographic, 'How geckos stick' (setae split into millions of nanoscale spatulae; van der Waals attraction; nonstick coatings like those on frying pans undermine their clinging; a wet surface such as a bathtub inhibits it) — https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/animals-science-geckos-reptiles-sticky

Wikipedia, Gecko feet (adhesion from van der Waals forces; about 14,000 setae per foot, each with about 1,000 spatulae) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gecko_feet ; gecko feet exude no glue, they exploit a weak molecular force — https://www.todayifoundout.com/?p=7427
beats.caption: Tokay geckos walk up walls and across glass, gripping with millions of microscopic tips on their toes. But there's one surface that beats them. Did you guess it? #gecko #tokaygecko #animalfacts #science

beats.say: But one surface beats them.
I went to find it.
Tokays grow about a foot long.
Some reach about forty centimeters.
Their name comes from their call.
To-kay!
It yelled that at me. Rude.
They also bite hard.
Big ones can pierce skin.
Tap like. I need a bandage.
Back to the surface. Guess one: glass?
Nope. Glass is easy.
Guess two: a smooth wall?
Nope. Walls are its whole thing.
Here's the thing. Look at its toes.
About fourteen thousand hairs per foot.
Each splits into about a thousand tips.
No glue. No suction cups.
Just a weak pull between molecules.
Times millions. Enough to hold its weight.
So the one surface?
A nonstick frying pan.
Nonstick coatings break the pull.
Wet surfaces mess it up too.
Like a bathtub.
So I hid in a frying pan.
Wait. That's where meatballs get cooked.
It hunts insects at night.
And sometimes small animals.
It even lives wild in Florida now.
Follow me. I'm finding a bathtub.
Threat to meatballs: medium.
What did you guess? Comment.
Glass frogs have see-through bellies.
beats.loop_say: So yes, I saw everything. Because
beats.comment: Would you want a see-through belly? 👇
beats.bonus: Resting glassfrogs pack about 89% of their red blood cells into the liver and become 2-3 times more transparent (Taboada et al. 2022, Science).
sources: Wikipedia, Glass frog (heart, liver and gut visible through the belly skin; you can watch the heart pump; 3-7.5 cm; males guard the eggs) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass_frog (checked 2026-10-25)

Taboada et al. 2022, Science: resting glassfrogs (Hyalinobatrachium fleischmanni) remove ~89% of red blood cells from circulation and pack them in the liver, increasing transparency 2-3x — https://pratt.duke.edu/news/glassfrogs-hide-red-blood-cells-their-liver-become-transparent/ ; https://www.amnh.org/explore/news-blogs/glassfrogs-camouflage
beats.caption: Flip a glass frog over and you can watch its heart pump. While it sleeps, it hides almost 90% of its red blood cells in its liver to turn even clearer. #glassfrog #frogs #animalfacts #science

beats.say: You can watch its heart pump.
So I looked for its feelings.
Just organs. Zero feelings.
When it sleeps, it hides its blood.
Almost ninety percent of its red cells.
Packed into its liver.
It turns two to three times clearer.
I tried. I'm still a meatball.
Like and follow. I'm getting a mirror.
Want a see-through belly? Comment.
Nine-banded armadillos have identical quadruplets.
beats.loop_say: So I still can't tell them apart. Because
beats.short_title: Armadillos Are Born as Identical Quadruplets 🐣
beats.comment: Could you tell armadillo quadruplets apart? 👇
beats.bonus: Despite the myth, nine-banded armadillos can't roll into a ball. Only three-banded armadillos can.
sources: Wikipedia, Nine-banded armadillo (the blastocyst splits into four identical embryos sharing one placenta; holds its breath up to six minutes; crosses rivers by inflating its intestines to float or by sinking and running across the riverbed; when startled can jump 91-120 cm (3-4 ft) straight up; cannot roll itself into a ball, unlike three-banded armadillos) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine-banded_armadillo (checked 2026-10-25)
beats.caption: A nine-banded armadillo's single embryo splits into four, so every litter is identical quadruplets. Startled, they can jump 3-4 feet straight up. #armadillo #animalfacts #wildlife #science

beats.say: One embryo splits into four.
So I tried to tell them apart.
I startled one. It jumped straight up.
Three to four feet.
It holds its breath for six minutes.
Then walks across the riverbed.
And it can't roll into a ball.
I can. It's my whole thing.
Like and follow. I'm working on my jump.
Could you tell them apart? Comment.
Lyrebirds steal other birds' songs.
beats.loop_say: So never trust a lyrebird's alarm. Because
beats.comment: What did you guess the sound was? 👇
beats.bonus: Male superb lyrebirds fake the alarm calls of a mobbing flock during courtship (Dalziell et al. 2021, Current Biology).
sources: Wikipedia, Superb lyrebird (70-80% of male vocalisations are imitations, mostly of other birds such as laughing kookaburras, whipbirds and shrike-thrushes; Attenborough's Life of Birds showed a male copying a car alarm, a chainsaw and camera shutters, two of the three filmed birds were captive; male tail of 16 feathers up to 70 cm, fanned forward over his body and head in display; dirt display mounds defended from other males; foraging moves up to ~200 tonnes of litter and soil per hectare per year) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superb_lyrebird (checked 2026-10-25)

Dalziell et al. 2021, Current Biology, 'Male lyrebirds create a complex acoustic illusion of a mobbing flock during courtship and copulation' (the fake mobbing-flock alarm comes when a female tries to leave the display arena or during copulation; the authors interpret it as deceptive) — https://cals.cornell.edu/news/2021/02/male-lyrebirds-snare-mates-acoustic-illusion ; https://news.mongabay.com/2021/03/male-superb-lyrebirds-master-mimics-found-to-trick-females-into-mating/
Australian ten-cent coin: reverse shows a male superb lyrebird (Stuart Devlin, 1966) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_ten-cent_coin
beats.caption: Up to 80% of a male superb lyrebird's song is copied from other animals. But one fake sound is the strangest of all. #lyrebird #birds #animalfacts

beats.say: But one fake sound is the strangest.
I went to hear it.
Up to 80 percent is copied.
Kookaburras. Whipbirds. Shrike-thrushes.
I sang him my best song.
He did not copy me.
Is the strange sound a chainsaw?
One did that on TV.
Fine print: mostly zoo birds.
Tap like. I'm getting closer.
The male's tail has sixteen feathers.
He flips it over his head.
Then dances on a dirt stage.
I tried to join. He chased me off.
So is it a camera shutter?
Close. Still not it.
But wait. Watch when a female leaves.
He fakes a whole flock in a panic.
Like a predator is right there.
Scientists think it makes her stay.
That's not romance. That's a scam.
They also dig. A lot.
Up to 200 tonnes of soil.
Per hectare. Every year.
That is a lot of gardening.
He's on Australia's ten-cent coin.
I'm worth less than that.
Follow me. I'm learning a new sound.
Threat to meatballs: low.
Threat to my ego: high.
What did you guess? Comment.
One puffin held sixty-two fish at once.
beats.loop_say: So never tell a puffin you're a fish. Because
beats.short_title: One Puffin Carried 62 Fish at Once 🐟
beats.comment: How many fish could you carry in your mouth? 👇
beats.bonus: Puffins shed the bright outer plates of their beaks after the breeding season.
sources: BirdLife International, Seabird of the month: Atlantic Puffin (average catch around 10 fish per trip; record in Britain 62 fish at once) — https://www.birdlife.org/news/2022/04/06/seabird-of-the-month-atlantic-puffin-fratercula-arctica/ ; Audubon Project Puffin FAQ — https://hogisland.audubon.org/puffin-faqs-0

Wikipedia, Atlantic puffin (holds earlier catches in place with its muscular, grooved tongue; serrated beak edges help retain fish; top flight speed about 80 km/h (50 mph); bright bill plates and facial ornaments are shed in a partial moult after breeding) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_puffin (checked 2026-10-25)
beats.caption: Puffins usually bring back about 10 fish a trip, but one in Britain held 62 at once. A grooved tongue pins the fish while it catches more. #puffin #birds #animalfacts #seabirds

beats.say: So I asked if it had room.
Its grooved tongue pins the first catch.
Spiky beak edges hold the rest.
It went for one more.
It flies up to fifty miles an hour.
And that bright beak? Seasonal.
After breeding, the bright plates fall off.
It's a costume. I'm not.
Like and follow. I'm hiding from puffins.
How many could you carry? Comment.
Wood frogs freeze solid every winter.
beats.loop_say: So don't feel sorry for it. Because
beats.short_title: How Wood Frogs Survive Freezing Solid 🧊
beats.comment: What was your guess before the reveal? 👇
beats.bonus: Glucose from the liver and urea act as antifreeze, protecting the frog's cells while it is frozen.
sources: Wikipedia, Wood frog (survives losing 65-70% of total body water to ice; frozen frogs show no heartbeat, breathing, blood circulation or muscle movement; urea and glucose act as cryoprotectants; Alaskan frogs stayed frozen 193 +/- 11 consecutive days; the only North American frog north of the Arctic Circle; usually a dark eye mask; adults 51-70 mm) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wood_frog (checked 2026-10-25)

National Park Service, Denali: amphibians (burrow into decaying leaves on the forest floor for winter; the liver turns glycogen into glucose when freezing starts, glucose lowers the freezing point inside cells; the frogs freeze solid, don't breathe and their hearts don't beat; core organs like the heart and liver freeze last and thaw first; in spring they thaw and look for breeding ponds) — https://www.nps.gov/dena/learn/nature/amphibians.htm
Scienceline, frozen frogs (heart slows and stops as the frog freezes; scientists aren't sure what restarts it) — https://scienceline.org/?p=1146
beats.caption: Wood frogs let up to 70% of their body water turn to ice, and their hearts stop all winter. So how do they wake up in spring? #woodfrog #frogs #animalfacts #science

beats.say: Hearts stop. So how do they wake?
I went to find out.
Up to seventy percent of it becomes ice.
No heartbeat. No breathing.
No blood moves at all.
Some stay frozen over 190 days.
I'd just be a freezer meal.
It even lives above the Arctic Circle.
The only North American frog up there.
Tap like. It keeps me warm.
So how does it survive? Guess one:
It flies south like the birds?
No. It hides under dead leaves.
Guess two: a tiny blanket?
I offered mine. It jumped on me.
But here's the thing. Look inside.
Its liver floods its body with sugar.
The sugar works like antifreeze.
It protects the cells from the ice.
Urea helps too. Yes, the pee stuff.
In spring, it thaws.
Its heart and liver thaw first.
Then it hops off to find a pond.
Nobody's fully sure what restarts the heart.
And look, it wears a mask.
Like a tiny bandit.
I tried the sugar trick.
Now I'm a glazed meatball.
Follow for more frozen secrets.
Threat to meatballs: zero.
What was your guess? Comment.
Mudskippers are fish that live on land.
beats.loop_say: So yes, it's still technically a fish. Because
beats.short_title: Mudskippers Are Fish That Live on Land 🐟
beats.comment: Is a mudskipper more fish or more frog? 👇
beats.bonus: A 2023 PNAS study found mudskippers blink by retracting their eyes, mostly when they are on land.
sources: Wikipedia, Mudskipper (spend up to three quarters of their life on land; breathe through skin and the lining of mouth and throat when wet; keep water in large gill chambers; eyes on top of the flat head; live in burrows in intertidal mud) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudskipper (checked 2026-10-25)

Aiello et al. 2023, PNAS, 'The origin of blinking in both mudskippers and tetrapods is linked to life on land' (blink by retracting the eyes into the sockets under a dermal cup, almost only on land) — https://www.psu.edu/news/eberly-college-science/story/blinking-fish-reveals-clues-how-our-ancestors-evolved-water-land
beats.caption: Mudskippers spend up to three quarters of their lives out of water. They breathe through wet skin, keep water in their gill chambers and blink by pulling their eyes into their heads. #mudskipper #fish #animalfacts

beats.say: Up to three quarters of their lives.
So I brought one a towel.
It breathes through its wet skin.
And keeps water in its gills.
Its eyes sit on top of its head.
It blinks by pulling them in.
Then it skipped right at me.
I'm a meatball. I can't even swim.
Like and follow. I'm out of towels.
Fish or frog? Comment.
Pangolins are armored against lions.
beats.loop_say: So yes, the armor was the problem. Because
beats.comment: What did you guess the weakness was? 👇
beats.bonus: In 2023 scientists described a new pangolin lineage, Manis mysteria, from seized scales alone. No one has seen one alive.
sources: Wikipedia, Pangolin (scales made of keratin, the material of human fingernails; curls into a ball when threatened; no teeth, swallowed stones grind food; large pangolins extend the tongue up to 40 cm; eats 140-200 g of insects a day; noxious anal-gland chemical like a skunk's; young cling to the mother's tail; the most trafficked mammals in the world) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangolin (checked 2026-10-25)

AP via WTOP, Feb 2026, 'These shy, scaly anteaters are the most trafficked mammals in the world' (armored ball that even lions struggle with, but no real defense against human hunters; more than half a million pangolins seized 2016-2024 per CITES) — https://wtop.com/asia/2026/02/these-shy-scaly-anteaters-are-the-most-trafficked-mammals-in-the-world/

CITES CoP17 (2016) moved all eight pangolin species to Appendix I, banning international commercial trade (in force January 2017) — https://news.mongabay.com/2016/09/commercial-trade-in-all-eight-pangolin-species-has-just-been-banned/ ; https://www.fws.gov/international-affairs/pangolins
Manis mysteria, described in PNAS 2023 from 27 scales seized in Hong Kong and 6 in Yunnan; no live animal documented — https://edition.cnn.com/2023/09/27/world/new-pangolin-species-discovery-scn
beats.caption: Pangolins wear armor made of keratin, the stuff in your fingernails, and even lions struggle to crack them. But they have exactly one weakness. #pangolin #animalfacts #wildlife #conservation

beats.say: But they have exactly one weakness.
So I went looking for it.
The scales are keratin.
Same stuff as your fingernails.
Weakness one: the soft belly?
Nope. It rolls into a ball.
Belly inside. Armor outside.
Even lions struggle to open it.
I knocked. Nobody answered.
Tap like. I'm still searching.
Weakness two: no teeth?
It really has zero teeth.
It swallows stones to grind its food.
And a tongue up to forty centimeters.
Not a weakness. Kind of genius.
Wait. What if the ball is the problem?
Lions can't open it.
But people just pick it up.
That's why it's the most trafficked mammal.
Over half a million seized in eight years.
Its armor works on everything but us.
Since 2017, global trade is banned.
Rolling up is my plan too.
I'm already a ball.
A delicious ball.
Good news: it only eats ants and termites.
I checked. I am not an ant.
Bonus: in 2023, scientists named a new pangolin.
From seized scales. Nobody's seen one alive.
Follow for the next weakness.
What did you guess? Comment.
Ladybugs look totally harmless.
beats.loop_say: So yes, I'm keeping my distance. Because
beats.comment: What did you guess the weapon was? 👇
beats.bonus: This defense is called reflex bleeding: a foul-tasting alkaloid fluid released from the leg joints.
sources: Wikipedia, Coccinella septempunctata (reflex bleeding: emits a foul-tasting alkaloid fluid from its leg joints; high-contrast black and orange spots deter predators; eats at least 24 species of aphid; larvae dark grey to black with tubercles; adults 6.5-7.8 mm; overwinter in clusters for warmth and protection, which also helps them find mates; national insect of Finland; established in the US in 1973 in New Jersey, apparently introduced accidentally via waste from JFK airport) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coccinella_septempunctata (checked 2026-10-25)
Ladybirds are beetles (order Coleoptera, family Coccinellidae), not true bugs — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coccinellidae
beats.caption: Ladybugs look harmless. They're not even bugs. And they hide one gross secret weapon. #ladybug #insects #animalfacts #bugs

beats.say: But they hide one gross weapon.
I went to find it.
First, they're not bugs. They're beetles.
This one has seven spots.
About seven millimeters long.
Smaller than me. Way scarier.
It eats aphids. Lots of aphids.
At least twenty-four kinds.
Its babies look like tiny alligators.
Same species. I checked twice.
I did not get close to those.
Tap like. I'm getting closer.
Is the weapon its bite?
Nope. It ignored me completely.
Then is it the spots?
Close. Those colors are a warning.
But a warning of what?
Wait. I poked it.
It bled from its knees. On purpose.
It's called reflex bleeding.
The fluid tastes foul.
Packed with bitter alkaloids.
Predators learn the colors. Then avoid them.
My defense is smelling like garlic.
In winter, they huddle in clusters.
For warmth. And to find a date.
It's Finland's national insect.
Finland picked the knee bleeder.
It reached the US by accident.
Apparently through airport trash. In 1973.
Follow me. I'm washing my hands.
Threat to meatballs: low. Gross factor: high.
What did you guess? Comment.
